planting.note: Broadcast or drill at 25-40 lbs/acre in October into a well-drained bed; inoculate with pea/vetch-group rhizobium if the site has no recent vetch history.

directions: Released by the Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station at Auburn as a common-vetch selection bred for better cold tolerance, earlier spring vigor, and resistance to root-knot and soybean-cyst nematodes compared to older common-vetch lines, making it a frequent Southeast and Gulf Coast alternative to hairy vetch. Mow or crimp at early-to-mid bloom in spring before pods harden to maximize nitrogen release and prevent volunteer reseeding, then let residue wilt one to two weeks before incorporating or no-till planting the next crop.
sources: UC Davis SAREP Cover Crop Database
Southern Cover Crops Council Cover Crop Information Sheet - Vetch, Common
UF/IFAS Cool-Season Forage Variety Recommendations for Florida

planting.note: Seed in fall once soil has cooled, ahead of cotton, into well-drained soil across the Florida Panhandle, south Georgia, Alabama, or the Carolinas; inoculate with lupine-specific rhizobium.

directions: A low-alkaloid, 'sweet' white lupine released by USDA-ARS at Tifton, Georgia, bred specifically as a winter cover crop ahead of cotton across the lower Southeast. Its deep taproot breaks up compaction while historically supplying around 100 kg of nitrogen per hectare to a following corn crop. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or herbicide at early bloom, since unterminated plants can reseed and persist as a volunteer weed.
sources: Purdue New Crop Resources - White Lupin: An Alternate Crop for the Southern Coastal Plain
Southern Cover Crops Council Cover Crop Information Sheet - Lupin, White

planting.note: Broadcast at 20-30 lbs/acre in early fall, or scatter lightly under trees or vines at garden scale, and let it scramble through winter as a row-middle cover.

directions: Released in 1956 by the California Agricultural Experiment Station from Turkish plant material, this remains the classic orchard and vineyard row-middle cover crop, fixing nitrogen unusually fast, often within about a week of emergence. Mow or crimp at first bloom to release 100-300 lbs of nitrogen per acre along with roughly 8,000 lbs per acre of weed-suppressing dry-matter mulch.
sources: NRCS Plant Materials release notice - 'Lana' Woollypod Vetch
SARE Managing Cover Crops Profitably - Woollypod Vetch
UC Davis SAREP Cover Crop Database

planting.note: Broadcast at 2-4 lbs/1000 sq ft in spring into marginal, droughty, or alkaline ground where true clovers struggle; inoculate with Melilotus/Medicago-group rhizobium.

directions: The first low-coumarin yellow sweetclover, the result of a 22-year Agriculture Canada breeding program at Saskatoon, bred to avoid the 'sweetclover bleeding disease' risk of moldy high-coumarin hay. As a biennial it forms a rosette and deep taproot in its first year, then bolts and flowers in its second, valued as a deep-rooting soil builder and pollinator planting on ground too marginal for true clovers. Mow before second-year seed-set to prevent volunteer spread.
sources: NRCS Plant Guide - Yellow Sweetclover and White Sweetclover
Canadian Journal of Plant Science - NORGOLD: A Low Coumarin Yellow Blossom Sweetclover

planting.note: Broadcast on a warm, well-drained bed in late spring between widely spaced warm-season crops; rarely needs inoculation since it nodulates with cowpea-group rhizobium already common in southern soils.

directions: An Australian-bred tetraploid Caribbean stylo naturalized in southern Florida and used throughout the tropics and subtropics as a drought-tolerant, nitrogen-fixing ground cover between widely spaced warm-season row crops. North of true zone 9 it behaves as a reseeding warm-season annual rather than a perennial, since hard freezes kill top growth. Let it self-reseed each fall instead of tilling in, since light grazing or mowing extends stand life.
sources: ECHO (North Fort Myers, FL) Plant Information Sheet - Caribbean Stylo
CSIRO Register of Australian Herbage Plant Cultivars - Verano

planting.note: Direct-seed in spring after frost risk passes, since it lacks canola or rapeseed-level winter hardiness; mow or crimp at flowering if growing as cover rather than for oilseed harvest.

directions: Released by Purdue University in 1973 from Swedish and Ethiopian Crambe germplasm, Meyer became the foundation cultivar for North Dakota's short-lived industrial crambe-oil industry and is still cited as the benchmark check variety in crambe trials. This fast, 80-to-100-day Brassicaceae relative of cabbage produces a dense, weed-suppressing canopy as a short-season rotational cover between main crops. Mow or crimp at flowering to prevent volunteer shatter if not harvesting for oilseed.
sources: Purdue NewCROP Proceedings - Crambe: A North Dakotan Case Study
Agronomy (MDPI) - Crambe (Crambe abyssinica Hochst): A Non-Food Oilseed Crop with Great Potential
